The reason I stress the ZK prover angle so much is:

We have a goal to maximize L1 gas limit, subject to complying with decentralization goals, which realistically we will formalize into something that includes a statement like "any operation that ethereum needs to get done, you can do on hardware that costs $X and runs on Y watts and needs Z bandwidth"

excerpts.author: daniellehrner
excerpts.content:
The precompile approach does not work well. We’ve found 3 consensus bugs in the BLS precompiles after we hardforked public testnets. Who knows how many more are lurking there and are threating liveness.

EVMMAX takes core devs out of the decision process what is supported on mainnet. App devs wouldn’t have to wait for several years until we decide to add SECP256R1 or Poseidon and could add it themselves. For me it’s a strict improvement for app devs

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: It’s also an advantage for L2s as precompiles are often far more computationally expensive than their gas suggests when run in fault proof systems and so wind up being “accelerated” by actually calling out to the L1 precompile but that adds a bunch of complexity and means special handling. Doing it inside the EVM would be much simpler.

excerpts.author: daniellehrner
excerpts.content: That seems like a new EOF debacle in the making. EF researchers decide early to go down a path that is very controversial, centralising block building in this case, without seeking outside feedback if that is even acceptable for the community. The only thing we get is hints from time to time on social media. Tons of time and resources are spent working on it and it might just be rejected, because centralising block building might be something that home stakers will never accept.

excerpts.author: gakonst
excerpts.content: Block building as-is emerged downstream of solving another user issue which was more important, reverting transactions and sandwiching. It was pretty well thought out IMO and a necessary evil with ways to escape down the line via FOCIL..

excerpts.author: gakonst
excerpts.content: It is and it isn't right? What are the crypto primitives you'd like to see? Are they actually that many? And what is the gas cost you'd expect them to have vs a precompile, and how much more effort is it to make it efficient in the evm level (eg if it also required evm simd to be fast)? There are can of worms stuff that are just poor ROI...

excerpts.author: tersec

excerpts.author: xrchz
excerpts.content: Formal verification is possible on status quo EVM. It's simply not true that EOF is required for verification.

excerpts.author: daniellehrner
excerpts.content:
You can remove reverted txs from block building from Reth today, nobody is stopping you. Deal with the potential DOS issue and its done. No need for centralised block building.

There are alternatives to sandwiching by block builders: Let smart contracts define their own transaction order rules. If block builders don't follow them the block is invalid. Sandwiching can still happen, but now instead of block builders sandwiching anonymous people, the apps will sandwich their own users and drive them to competitors if they abuse that. No need for centralised block building.

Today we have more than 10.000 nodes that can build blocks on Ethereum, once we centralise we'll have less than 10 (looking at Bitcoin). We risk Ethereum's 100% uptime if we reduce the number of block builder by orders of magnitudes. How is that a user-centric approach?

excerpts.author: daniellehrner
excerpts.content: I am not claiming to have all the answers, but it seems centralised block building is the only way that is being researched.
